q7.answer: The API encrypts the raw token with an application key and stores only the ciphertext in the email job. The worker decrypts it with the same key, builds the link as {PUBLIC_BASE_URL}/reset?t=<token>, and sends it, so the raw token exists only in the job ciphertext and the email.

q8.answer: The server computes SHA-256 of the token from the URL, looks up password_reset_tokens by token_hash, and checks that used_at and revoked_at are NULL and expires_at is after now(). The page-load check and the submit check use this same test, and the submit check runs again under a row lock.

q9.answer: There is no separate counter. The count is a query over password_reset_tokens rows for that user_id with created_at in the last hour, taken under the account row lock. Rows age out of the window by time, and the 24-hour purge is far longer than the 1-hour window, so it never removes rows the count still needs.

q10.answer: When a new link is issued, in the same request transaction as the insert, the server sets revoked_at on all of that account's unused tokens. Older links then fail the valid-token check, and any queued job for them is skipped by the worker's superseded check.

q11.answer: In one transaction the server updates users.password_hash, sets used_at on the token, revokes the account's other tokens, deletes all of the user's sessions, and inserts the 'password changed' job, then commits; the redirect to /login comes after the commit. The confirmation email is therefore queued only if the reset committed, though this holds only if the queue is in Postgres, which is still open question 3.

q12.answer: Step 4 runs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the token row inside BEGIN and re-checks validity under that lock. The second submit waits, then sees used_at set and gets the expired page, so only one transaction applies the password change; the hashing before BEGIN can run twice but writes nothing.
